newsitem.headline: RTRS-AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

AMLC COMMENTARY: Higher U.S. feeder steer prices will work in Australia's favour by increasing the production cost of U.S. beef and making it less competitive in export markets.
Higher U.S. steer prices signal producers to re-build herds.
Producers are likely to retain more replacement heifers, further reducing the supply of feeder steers and pushing prices higher again, continuing the cycle.

This message emerged from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) January U.S. cattle inventory report, released last Friday. The report contained important messages for the Australian beef industry.
As a result of higher slaughter levels throughout 1996, U.S. cattle numbers are on the way down.
The USDA estimated the U.S. herd had been reduced by 2.3 million head, down from the revised January 1 1996 inventory of 103.5 million head.

The majority of the reduction has been in cows and heifers, the "engine room" of beef production. Cow numbers fell by more than one million head to 43.6 million while replacement heifers were down by two percent. Liquidation has not finished, with heifers tagged to move into feedlots up by three percent.
This will mean fewer replacement heifers with the effect of reduced feeder steer supplies to be largely negated by the increased availability of feeder heifers.
In effect this will alleviate the effect of any tightening in this year's feeder supplies. Feeder prices are likely to remain subdued and encourage produers to downsize herds.

U.S. feeder steer supplies will begin to tighten from the beginning of 1998 after the large cow kill in 1996. Inventories of cattle under 250 kg liveweight at the beginning of 1997 were down by 4.3 percent compared with the previous year. Lower numbers of these cattle means that from early 1998 feedlotters will have to compete more afggressively for lower supplies.
In the immediate market, a stronger U.S. market and a lower Australian dollar are being countered by further price falls in the Japanese market.
In Australia, saleyard price movements are positive as the market readjusts after the recent good rains across the eastern seaboard.

U.S. prices for imported beef traded higher in the latest week, moving prices closer to those of domestically produced beef. Lean trimmings prices moved two-three cents US a lb higher with 90CL finishing the week at 83 UScents a lb.
With the further depreciation of the Australian currency during the week, prices reached 206 Australian cents a kg.
This represents the highest return to Australian exporters of this type of beef since February 1996.
Strength in U.S. manufacturing beef prices is despite large U.S. slaughter levels in recent weeks.
Total slaughter for the week to February 6 was up nine percent compared with last year, while in the previous week cow slaughter was up five percent compared with a year ago.

The Japanese market continues to struggle under the weight of the yen depreciation. Although the chilled grassfed fullsets wholesale price is currently at the same U.S. dollar denominated rates as in March 1996, at 151 US cents a lb, in yen terms the price is now 85 yen a kg higher.
The weakening of the yen has increased the price of imported beef for Japanese consumers and also created uncertainty among Japanese traders, restricting the trade.

While export offer prices continue to fall, with chilled grassfed fullset prices down by five US cents a lb to 137 US cents a lb, traders have been slow in committing to forward orders. This has created a large differential between export offer prices and Japanese wholesale prices, with the differential now at 14 US cents a lb for grassfed fullsets.

Australian beef exports to Japan for January, at 20,186 tonnes, were similar to last year. Total January shipments, at 48,790 tonnes, eclipsed the January 1996 level of 45,161 tonnes. This was due to higher sales to the manufacturing beef markets of the U.S. and Canada, which imported 9,520 and 3,400 tonnes respectively.
Increased processor demand assisted price rises in Australian eastern state saleyards over the week.

Bullock prices rose five to seven cents a kg to an average 99 cents a kg liveweight in Queensland. In New South Wales they rose nine cents a kg to 94 cents a kg while in Victoria they rose 1.5 cents a kg to 85 cents a kg.
Increased restocker interest helped cow prices while feedlotters were more active in sourcing cattle.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
